questions.subject: JAVA_PROGRAMMING
questions.topic: What a lambda expression is at run time
questions.learningObjective: state that a lambda is an object of its target interface and nothing else

options.text: true:false - a lambda is an object of the single interface it was written for, and of no other type.
true:true - every object also implements Runnable through the default method inheritance of Object.
options.misconception: believes all objects implement common interfaces

options.text: false:false - a lambda has no run-time type, so it matches no interface at all.
options.misconception: believes a lambda is not an object

options.text: Compile error - a lambda may not be widened to Object by an assignment.
options.misconception: believes a lambda cannot be stored in a general reference

questions.explanation: The rule is that a lambda expression creates an object that implements its target functional interface and nothing else, so the type test against Op succeeds and the one against Runnable does not; widening the reference to Object is legal and loses only the ability to call apply without a cast. The compiler typically synthesises a class for the lambda, which is exactly why there is a run-time type to ask about. Option C is the intuition that a lambda is syntax rather than a value, and it is worth testing because the syntax really does look like a fragment of a method.
questions.hint: A lambda has a target type, and that type is what it implements.

questions.subject: JAVA_PROGRAMMING
questions.topic: Capturing a local that was reassigned
questions.learningObjective: repair a lambda that captures a local which is not effectively final

options.text: final int captured = base; Op op = () -> captured;  freezes the value before capturing it.
Op op = () -> base;  captures the local directly, which is what the compiler refuses here.
options.misconception: believes a local may be captured after it changes

options.text: Op op = () -> seed * 10;  recomputes from the parameter, so the increment is left out.
options.misconception: believes recomputing the expression reproduces the captured value

options.text: Op op = () -> base + 1;  applies the adjustment again inside the lambda body.
options.misconception: believes the captured value was the pre-adjustment one

questions.explanation: The rule is that a local may be captured only if it is effectively final, meaning never assigned after its initialisation, and base is assigned twice, so the capture must go through a new variable that is not. Copying the adjusted value into a final local and capturing that gives 21, which is the number the code computes. Option C is the tempting shortcut because it uses the parameter instead and compiles, but the parameter is 2 and the expression gives 20, silently dropping the increment the caller was meant to pay.
questions.hint: A captured local must never change; copy it into one that does not.

questions.subject: JAVA_PROGRAMMING
questions.topic: Walking a hierarchy through reflection
questions.learningObjective: count the classes in a hierarchy by following getSuperclass

options.text: 4:B - the chain runs C, B, A and Object, and the parent of C is B.
3:B - the loop stops at A, so Object is never counted as part of the chain.
options.misconception: believes the root of a class hierarchy is null rather than Object

options.text: 4:A - getSuperclass reports the topmost class of the hierarchy rather than the parent.
options.misconception: believes getSuperclass walks to the root

options.text: Compile error - a Class value may not be used in a loop update expression.
options.misconception: believes a Class value cannot be assigned to a variable

questions.explanation: The rule is that getSuperclass returns the direct parent and returns null once the chain reaches Object and is asked again, so a loop that keeps going counts all four classes here and stops at the null. The second half of the output is a single step of the same walk, which reports B because that is C's direct parent rather than the root of the hierarchy. Option B is the misconception that the loop is at fault for stopping, when in fact the null is the documented end of the chain and Object is a real class that any class hierarchy includes.
questions.hint: Ask whether the end of the chain is null or the root class.

questions.subject: JAVA_PROGRAMMING
questions.topic: The reflective form of the is-a test
questions.learningObjective: predict what isAssignableFrom reports for a class and a subclass instance

options.text: true:true - a Dog is assignable to both its own type and the type it extends.
true:false - a class accepts its supertypes but never its own exact type.
options.misconception: believes a class is not assignable to itself

options.text: false:false - the reflective test compares the two types by identity, not by subtyping.
options.misconception: believes isAssignableFrom is an identity comparison

options.text: false:true - the arguments are supplied in the opposite order to the method's name.
options.misconception: believes the receiver class is the one being tested

questions.explanation: The rule is that the receiver of isAssignableFrom is the supertype side of the question, so asking whether Animal accepts Dog is true and asking whether Dog accepts Dog is also true because a type is assignable to itself. That is the whole meaning of the is-a relation expressed reflectively, and it is the same answer the compiler would give for an ordinary assignment. Option D is the trap in the naming, since the two classes are written in the order supertype then subtype, and reading the call as though the first argument were the subject is an easy slip.
questions.hint: The class you call the method on is the one doing the accepting.

questions.subject: JAVA_PROGRAMMING
questions.topic: One array holding two levels of the hierarchy
questions.learningObjective: count the elements of a base-typed array that pass a subtype test

options.text: 1 - a Dog is an Animal as well as a Dog, so the test accepts it and rejects the plain one.
0 - a type test fails whenever the declared type of the element is the supertype.
options.misconception: believes a test fails if the reference is declared as a supertype

options.text: 2 - the array's declared element type makes every element pass a test for one of its subtypes.
options.misconception: believes the array's declared type decides the test

options.text: Compile error - a Dog may not be placed in an array of Animal.
options.misconception: believes widening into an array is not allowed

questions.explanation: The rule is that a subtype instance is an instance of every type above it, so the first element passes the Dog test and the second does not, which gives 1. The declared type of the loop variable matters only for what the compiler lets the body call, and after the test the binding is a Dog, so the counter is incremented for exactly one element. Option B is the misconception that a wide reference hides the object's real type, and it is the same confusion that makes people expect a field read to dispatch the way a method call does.
questions.hint: Ask what the object is, not what the variable was declared as.

questions.subject: JAVA_PROGRAMMING
questions.topic: A base-typed parameter that reaches a subtype-only method
questions.learningObjective: trace a guard that makes a subtype-only call available inside a base-typed method

options.text: dog:ball - the test narrows the reference, and both calls then reach the Dog implementation.
animal:animal - a base-typed parameter keeps the base body for every call it makes.
options.misconception: believes the parameter's type controls which body runs

options.text: dog:animal - describe dispatches to the override but fetch is taken from the base type.
options.misconception: believes a narrowed reference only helps the first call

options.text: Compile error - fetch is not declared in the parameter's type, so the call is rejected.
options.misconception: believes a type test does not make subtype members available

questions.explanation: The rule is that the pattern test narrows the reference for the rest of the branch, so inside it the parameter is a Dog and both the overridden describe and the Dog-only fetch are callable, giving dog and ball. Outside the branch the reference is still an Animal, which is why the fallback call is legal where fetch would not be. Option D is the misconception that a base-typed variable is permanently limited to the base's members, and this narrowing is the standard way to write code that has to cope with a subtype it was not promised.
questions.hint: Ask what the reference is called inside the branch and outside it.

questions.subject: JAVA_PROGRAMMING
questions.topic: An exact class test used where a subtype test was meant
questions.learningObjective: repair a membership test that compares class objects instead of testing the type

options.text: static boolean isDog(Animal a) { return a instanceof Dog; }  tests membership, so a Puppy also passes.
static boolean isDog(Animal a) { return a.getClass() == Dog.class; }  keeps the class comparison, which excludes subclasses.
options.misconception: believes a class comparison includes every subclass

options.text: static boolean isDog(Animal a) { return a.getClass() == Animal.class; }  compares against the base class instead.
options.misconception: believes the base class identifies every animal as a dog

options.text: static boolean isDog(Animal a) { return a.getClass().getSuperclass() == Dog.class; }  walks one level up before comparing.
options.misconception: believes membership is a property of the parent class

questions.explanation: The rule is that class objects compare by identity, so getClass() == Dog.class is true only for a Dog and never for a Puppy, whereas instanceof tests the is-a relation and accepts the whole subtree, giving true for both. The marked line is a bug precisely because the two look interchangeable and only one of them means the sentence a reader hears. Option D is worth noticing as well: comparing the parent class would pass the Puppy and fail the Dog, which is the mirror image of the same confusion about what a class value identifies.
questions.hint: Ask whether the test should include the subclasses of the type it names.

questions.subject: JAVA_PROGRAMMING
questions.topic: A visitor that dispatches twice per element
questions.learningObjective: trace a design where the element and the visitor both choose a method

options.text: bookcd - each element picks accept from its own class, then the visitor picks by argument type.
bookbook - the visitor instance is shared, so every element reaches the same method.
options.misconception: believes a visitor's method choice depends on the visitor's state

options.text: cdcd - the accept call is resolved against the array's declared element type, which is Item.
options.misconception: believes the declared interface type picks the accept body

options.text: Compile error - an interface may not declare a method that takes another interface as a parameter.
options.misconception: believes interfaces cannot reference one another

questions.explanation: The rule is that each element class supplies its own accept, so the first call already selects Book's body, and that body passes this along, which lets the visitor choose between its two visit methods by the argument's type; two dispatches in sequence is what makes a new operation possible without changing the item classes. The answer that one dispatch would be enough is the misconception behind the whole design, since a single virtual call can only choose on the receiver. Option C is the ordinary single-dispatch intuition applied to the first call, and the program is built so that intuition has to be extended.
questions.hint: Two calls, each choosing a body from a different receiver.

questions.topic: A chain of type tests over a hierarchy of three levels
questions.learningObjective: compute the result of a chain of subtype tests over an array

options.text: dog:ball|cat:nap|animal:none| - each element takes the first branch its own type satisfies.
animal:none|animal:none|animal:none| - a base-typed element never satisfies a subtype test.
options.misconception: believes a base-typed reference cannot pass a subtype test

options.text: dog:ball|cat:nap|dog:ball| - the third element falls back to the first branch's result.
options.misconception: believes an unmatched element reuses the previous match

options.text: dog:ball|cat:nap|animal:none| without the trailing bar, since the loop skips the last append.
options.misconception: believes a loop appends once fewer time than it iterates

questions.explanation: The rule is that each test is evaluated against the object and the first satisfied branch is taken, so the dog uses its own name and the extra method, the cat takes the second branch, and the plain animal falls through to the final return, with a bar appended after every element including the last. Option B is the recurring misconception about base-typed references, and the whole array exists to make it visible: the variable is typed Animal in every iteration while the tests still tell the three values apart.
questions.hint: Work element by element and note the first branch each one satisfies.

questions.subject: JAVA_PROGRAMMING
questions.topic: Claims about dispatching on two different types
questions.learningObjective: judge which statements describe what a second dispatch adds
questions.stem: A call to item.accept(visitor) ends up in the visit method matching the item's type, even though the variable holding the item is typed as the Item interface. A cheat sheet lists four claims about that. Which claims are true? Select all that apply.

options.text: The call reaches the accept implementation belonging to the item's own runtime class.
A second call is needed, because one virtual call can consult only its own receiver's type.
One dispatch suffices, because the compiler merges the receiver's type with the argument's type.
options.misconception: believes the compiler combines both types into a single choice

options.text: The visitor matches on the argument's static type and refuses anything it cannot match exactly.
options.misconception: believes the visitor resolves against the static type

options.text: The item class stores the name of the visit method to call, so it selects the operation for itself.
options.misconception: believes the item class picks the visit method by name

questions.explanation: The rule is that a virtual call chooses a body from the runtime type of its own receiver, so the first call reaches the item's accept and the second call, whose receiver is the visitor, is what chooses between the visit methods by the argument's type; two receivers are involved because two types have to be consulted. The three wrong claims each try to collapse that into a single decision: the compiler merging the two types, the visitor matching statically rather than dynamically, or the item class naming a method for itself, none of which is how a run-time choice between two objects is made. That is the whole reason the pattern exists rather than adding a method to every item class.
questions.hint: Ask which receiver each of the two calls consults.

questions.subject: JAVA_PROGRAMMING
questions.topic: A sealed expression tree evaluated in two modes
questions.learningObjective: compute two different reductions of the same sealed hierarchy

options.text: 3:9 - the size mode counts the three leaves while the other mode adds their values.
9:3 - the mode string selects which of the two numbers is printed first.
options.misconception: believes the mode swaps the values rather than the strategy

options.text: 2:9 - a size reduction counts the top-level Add nodes, of which there is one.
options.misconception: believes size counts the internal nodes

options.text: Compile error - a switch over a sealed type may not call itself recursively in a case body.
options.misconception: believes a case body may not contain a recursive call

questions.explanation: The rule is that a case body may compute anything, including a recursive call, and the mode parameter is the second dimension of variation, so the size run reaches each leaf and returns 1 three times for 3 while the sum run returns the leaf values and adds them to 9. The permits clause means the switch needs no default, so both modes are handled by the same two cases. Option C is a reasonable-looking alternative definition of size, and it is exactly the kind of ambiguity that a parameter spelled as a string rather than a type leaves open.
questions.hint: Count the leaves for one run and add their values for the other.

questions.topic: Behaviour stored in a map and chosen by key
questions.learningObjective: trace a routing table that maps keys to interface implementations

options.text: A:aB:b - the key selects the implementation, and each one prefixes the key it was given.
A:aA:a - a map stores one value per type, so both lookups reach the first lambda.
options.misconception: believes a map keeps one value regardless of the key

options.text: a:b - the lambda parameter shadows the key, so the prefix never appears.

options.text: Compile error - a lambda may not be stored as a map value for an interface type.
options.misconception: believes lambdas cannot be fields or collection values

Nothing about storing the behaviour in a map changes how the call is resolved. Option B is the misconception that a map ignores its keys, and it is worth testing because the pattern looks like configuration while behaving exactly like a field holding an object.
questions.hint: Ask which value each lookup finds and what that value's body returns.

questions.subject: JAVA_PROGRAMMING
questions.topic: What an interface-typed reference may call
questions.learningObjective: state that the reference's type, not the object's, decides the callable members

options.text: 6 - apply is declared in the interface, so the call is legal and the implementation supplies the body.
9 - the reference is an interface, so it calls the implementation's own extra method instead.
options.misconception: believes an interface reference reaches every method of the object

options.text: Compile error - extra is not in the interface, so no method of Doubler may be called here.
options.misconception: believes an interface reference cannot call the method it declares

options.text: null - an interface-typed reference holds no object, so the call has no receiver.
options.misconception: believes an interface reference is not an object reference

questions.explanation: The rule is that the compiler checks a call against the declared type of the reference, so only apply is available here and the implementation's own extra method would need a cast or a differently typed variable, while the body that runs is still the implementation's. The declared type limits what can be said and never what will happen, which is the distinction the interface exists to draw. Option B is the misconception that runs the whole unit backwards, from the object outward rather than from the reference inward.
questions.hint: The reference's type is the compiler's view; the object supplies the behaviour.

questions.subject: JAVA_PROGRAMMING
questions.topic: A captured field read when the lambda runs
questions.learningObjective: predict that a lambda reads a captured field at call time

options.text: 7 - the lambda captures the object rather than a copy of the field, so it reads the new value.
5 - a lambda copies the values it uses, so the field is frozen when it is created.
options.misconception: believes a capture copies the current value

options.text: null - a field of a captured object cannot be read after the creating method returns.
options.misconception: believes a captured object's state expires with the method

options.text: Compile error - a field may not be read from inside a lambda body in another class.
options.misconception: believes a lambda cannot read its creator's fields

questions.explanation: The rule is that a lambda captures a reference to the enclosing instance, not a snapshot of its state, so the field read happens when apply runs and finds the value that was assigned most recently, which is 7. Contrast this with a local variable, which must be effectively final precisely because a capture of a changing local would be ambiguous, whereas a field's value is expected to change and the lambda simply observes it. Option B is the misconception that a capture is a copy, and it is a reasonable one to hold after learning that locals are frozen.
questions.hint: Ask whether the lambda holds the object or a copy of one field.

questions.subject: JAVA_PROGRAMMING
questions.topic: A call on a parameter inside a base method
questions.learningObjective: predict that a call on an argument dispatches on the argument's runtime type

options.text: woof - the call is made on the argument, so dispatch follows the argument's runtime type.
generic - a parameter is declared as the base type, so the base body is chosen.
options.misconception: believes a parameter's declared type selects the body

options.text: Compile error - a base class may not call an overridable method on a parameter.
options.misconception: believes calling an overridable method on a parameter is illegal

options.text: woof:generic - the call runs once for the argument and once for the enclosing object.
options.misconception: believes the enclosing object is also asked

questions.explanation: The rule is that a call on a reference dispatches on the runtime type of whatever that reference designates, and here the reference is the parameter, which holds a Dog, so the override runs. This is the deliberate contrast with the previous item, where the call had no receiver to examine beyond the class the body was written in. A base class is therefore free to pass a reference along and let the subtype decide, which is the mechanism behind most designs that keep the base ignorant of its subclasses.
questions.hint: Identify the receiver of the call before deciding anything.

questions.subject: JAVA_PROGRAMMING
questions.topic: A class constant that hides an interface constant
questions.learningObjective: repair a field that shadows an interface constant without changing it

options.text: static int LIMIT = Config.LIMIT;  copies the constant, so both names report the same value.
static int LIMIT = 9;  keeps a class constant of its own, which hides the interface one.
options.misconception: believes a class field changes the interface constant it shares a name with

options.text: static int LIMIT = Config.LIMIT + 1;  derives from the interface constant but adds to it.
options.misconception: believes a derived copy still counts as the same constant

options.text: int LIMIT = 9;  makes it an instance field, which the interface constant no longer collides with.
options.misconception: believes an instance field can satisfy an interface constant

questions.explanation: The rule is that an interface field is public, static and final, and a field declared in a class with the same name hides it for that class's own code while the interface's value is unchanged, so the two names can report different numbers. The marked line is a bug for that reason, and copying the interface constant restores a single reported value. Option D fails for a different reason worth noticing: the class does not need to declare anything at all, since it already inherits the constant, and adding an instance field of that name is both unnecessary and illegal to read from a static context.
questions.hint: A field of the same name hides the inherited one; it does not replace it.

questions.subject: JAVA_PROGRAMMING
questions.topic: Overload selection for an unbounded type variable
questions.learningObjective: predict that an unbounded type variable resolves an overload through Object

options.text: obj:obj - an unbounded type variable promises only Object, so both calls resolve to that overload.
str:obj - each call infers its own type argument, so the first reaches the String overload.
options.misconception: believes inference refines the body of an already-chosen call

options.text: str:str - both arguments are strings at run time, so the same overload is chosen twice.
options.misconception: believes overload selection consults the runtime type

options.text: Compile error - a type variable may not be passed where an overload set is available.
options.misconception: believes the compiler cannot resolve an overloaded call on a type variable

questions.explanation: The rule is that inside the method body the only thing known about an unbounded type variable is that it is some Object, and overload resolution has to be done once for the body rather than once per call, so the Object overload is the only signature the compiler can justify. Inference does happen at each call site, but it cannot retroactively give the body a more precise type, which is why the first call still prints obj even though a String was passed. Option B describes what most programmers expect and is the specific surprise this item exists to record.
questions.hint: Ask what the body knows about its own type variable, not what the caller passed.

questions.subject: JAVA_PROGRAMMING
questions.topic: A wildcard argument selecting a different overload
questions.learningObjective: predict that the argument's static type decides between two applicable overloads

options.text: int:wide - the first argument matches the narrower overload and the cast forces the wider one.
wide:wide - a wildcard in one signature makes the other signature inapplicable.
options.misconception: believes a wildcard overload rules out the specific one

options.text: int:int - the cast changes only the compiler's view, not which overload applies.
options.misconception: believes a cast does not affect overload selection

options.text: Compile error - a wildcard argument is not applicable to the wider overload.
options.misconception: believes a wildcard cannot be passed to a matching wildcard parameter

questions.explanation: The rule is that overload resolution picks the most specific applicable signature using the argument's static type, so a List<Integer> argument matches both signatures and the List<Integer> one is more specific, while the cast makes the argument a List of unknown numbers that only the wildcard signature accepts. Nothing about the object changes between the two calls, only what the compiler is told, which is the same rule that governs every overload in the language. Option C is the misconception that a cast is merely informational, and it is the cast that does the work here.
questions.hint: Compare the static type of each argument with the two signatures.
